saṁsāra
(‘roaming about [through births and rebirths]’)
------------------------------------------
According to हिन्दुइस्म्, though the आत्मन् (the सोउल् or the Self) is eternally free (nityamukta), it has somehow (inexplicably) got itself entangled with अविद्या (ignorance or nescience), which entanglement is stated to be anādi or beginning-less, though it can be ended (hence, sānta). This अविद्या leads to its perceiving द्वैत or duality, viz., the world and other beings as different from it. This again creates काम or desire in its मिन्द्, to get what it wants or get rid of what it does not want. To fulfil this काम it has to take repeated births. It is this transmigration that is called सṁसार.

saṁyama
(‘control’)
------------------------------------------
Though the word is used in the general sense of control or self-control, the Yogasūtras (3.4) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) employs it as a technical term.
When धारणा (fixing the मिन्द् on an object) and ध्यान (meditation on the same) result in समाधि (superconscious experience), the process (of practising these three together) is defined as सṁयम.
Patañjali describes a number of सिद्धिस् (psychic powers) that a योगि attains by practising सṁयम on various objects (3.5-55).

saṁskāras
(‘refinement’, ‘sacraments’)
------------------------------------------
The word saṁskāra, in a technical sense, means a ritualistic act (accompanied by appropriate mantras) by which a person is rid of his defects and limitations, and, made refined by adding some speciality.
Such सṁस्कारस् as listed in the smṛtis and धर्मशास्त्रस् vary from 16 to 40. However, 16 saṁskāras—generally called ṣoḍaśa-saṁskāras—have been widely accepted.
See ṢOḌAŚA-SAṀSKĀRAS for details.

Saṁnyāsa
(‘complete renunciation,’ ‘the order of मोन्क्स्’)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Ancient and medieval Hindu scriptures describe four āśramas or stages of life. (See ĀŚRAMA.) The last of these is सṁन्यास or the life of a recluse or a monk. Anyone who has developed an intense वैराग्य or spirit of renunciation for the world and is eager to attain मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्, is fit for taking सṁन्यास. However, in practice, it was restricted only to the ब्राह्मणस्.
One who takes the formal vows of सṁन्यास is called a saṁnyāsin.
There are four kinds of saṁnyāsins: कुटीचक, बहूदक, हṁस and parama-हṁस. (See PARAMAHAṀSA for details.) The last is considered as the best.
Procedure for taking Saṁnyāsa
The Dharmasindhu of Kāśīnātha Upādhye (A.

) sets out a procedure for taking सṁन्यास which is followed more or less even today.
Since सṁन्यास was taken either from the गार्हस्थ्य stage (as a householder) or from the वानप्रस्थ stage (as a forest recluse), this factor should be kept in मिन्द् while studying the same as given in the above-mentioned work.
Briefly stated, the procedure is as follows: seeking a competent saṁnyāsin-teacher and living with him for at least three months; purification of oneself through the जप of the गायत्री मन्त्र, Rudra and performance of कूष्माण्डहोम (vide Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.7) to get rid of sins; सङ्कल्प (religious resolve); śrāddha including to oneself; shaving, leaving the śikhā intact; getting the things needed for the saṁnyāsin’s life like ochre-cloth, दण्ड (staff), कमण्डलु (water pot), kaupīna (loincloth), pādukās (wooden sandals) and so on; worship of गणेश and performing Ābhyudayika śrāddha (See ĀBHYUDAYIKA-ŚRĀDDHA.); recital of certain Vedic texts; ड़स्तिन्ग्; सावित्रीप्रवेश (withdrawing the गायत्री मन्त्र into oneself since it will not be repeated after सṁन्यास); keeping vigil for the whole night; performance of विरजाहोम; burning of all wooden sacrificial vessels; blessing all the members of the family and leaving home; repeating the praiṣamantra (signifying total renunciation of hearth and home); offering of the śikhā (tuft of hair) and यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread) in water (or the fire of विरजाहोम); removal of the old clothes and accepting the ochre-clothes as well as other insignia of सṁन्यास from the गुरु; receiving the mahāvākya (See MAHĀVĀKYAS.) from the गुरु as also a new name; taking the blessings of the गुरु and the senior saṁnyāsins.
In some orders following non-advaitic tradition, the śikhā and the यज्ञोपवीत are kept intact and the जप of the गायत्री मन्त्र is continued.
Code of Conduct
The saṁnyāsin, after formally taking the vows of monastic life, has to lead a wandering life, not dwelling inside villages or towns. His stay should be outside, under a tree or a temple or an uninhabited होउसे. He can enter the village or the town for alms, only once in a day and that too after the smoke from the domestic hearths has died down. He should ever be on the move, wandering alone, never staying in the same place for more than three days, except during the rainy season. (See CĀTURMĀSYA.)
Observing strict celibacy and bathing thrice a day he must spend his time in जप (repetition of the divine name), ध्यान (meditation), surārcana (worship of his deity) whenever possible and contemplation on Vedāntic and devotional scriptures.
He should be controlled in eating (taking ड़ोओद् only once a day). Practising अहिṁसा (non-violence) and सत्य (truth), he should give abhaya (freedom from fear) to all creatures. He should be equanimous under all circumstances.
His possessions should be only those accepted during the taking of the monastic vows and hence should never accumulate things out of greed.
He should observe silence as much as possible and never practise अस्त्रोलोग्य् or occult sciences.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् are replete with many injunctions and prohibitions which may not appear to be relevant in the modern context.
Other Related Topics
There is no unanimity in the धर्म-śāstra whether सṁन्यास is allowed only to the ब्राह्मणस् or to other dvijas also.
An eccentric theory is sometimes put forward by the fanatical followers of Vedic rituals that only those who are physically disabled—and hence unable to perform the rituals—are fit for सṁन्यास!
Though शूद्रस् were denied सṁन्यास by the smṛtis and the medieval digests, śūdra-अस्चेतिच्स् did exist. Śaiva and शाक्त cults permitted it to them also.
Based on the Mahābhāṣya of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) one can surmise that women-अस्चेतिच्स् too existed, even in ancient days.
Dvijas who were critically ill and about to pass away could mentally utter the praiṣamantra and die as saṁnyāsins. (See ĀTURASAṀNYĀSA.)
After death, the body of a saṁnyāsin had to be buried.
Over the centuries, due to historical, sociological and civilisational factors several changes have been wrought in the institution of सṁन्यास though the old and orthodox orders continue to hold on to most of the ancient traditions. Some of them are: changes in modes of dress etc., like wearing stitched clothes and footwear; living in institutions and engaging in public service activities; performance of certain religious rites like पूजा and होम and so on.
Some orders of saṁnyāsins prefer च्रेमतिओन् after death, to बुरिअल्.
Conclusion
If the Hindu society has given the highest place of honour to the saṁnyāsins, it has also prescribed the highest standards of मोरलित्य्, एथिच्स् and spiritual values.
That the Hindu religion and the society are still vibrant and susceptible to further spiritual development is not a little due to these saṁnyāsins and the institution of सṁन्यास itself.
See also ASCETICS, ĀŚRAMA, DAŚA-NĀMĪS, MONASTICISM and YATI.

Saṁvargavidyā
(‘science of saṁvarga’)
------------------------------------------
See CHĀNDOGYA UPANIṢAD and VIDYĀS.

saṁhāra
(‘withdrawal,’ ‘destruction’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism posits a cyclic theory of च्रेअतिओन्. सृष्टि (creation), sthiti (sustenance) and सṁहार (withdrawal into the original cause) take place eternally in that cyclic order.
In सṁहार, the process is the exact reverse of सृष्टि.
The word is also used to indicate destruction or killing in general.
See also COSMOLOGY, LAYA and PRALAYA.

Saṁvarta-smṛti
------------------------------------------
Saṁvarta-smṛti seems to be a fairly ancient work. Saṁvarta is quoted by many authors of धर्मशास्त्रस् like अपरार्क, हरदत्त, मेधातिथि, विश्वरूप and others. As many as 200 verses of his, have been given in their works.
There is a printed text which appears to be an epitome of a portion of the original स्मृति of Saṁvarta.
The स्मृति is in the form of Saṁvarta’s teachings to वामदेव and others.
The topics dealt with may be summarised as follows:
Rules of conduct for a ब्रह्मचारिन्; prāyaścittas or expiations for various kinds of sins; duties of a householder, a forest hermit and a saṁnyāsin; special duties of a king; and a few minor topics as the age of girls for मर्रिअगे.
According to the Mahābhārata (Ādiparva 67) Saṁvarta was a son of Añgiras. बृहस्पति and Ucathya were his brothers.
It is difficult to say whether this was the same Saṁvarta who authored this स्मृति.

sāṁnāyya
(‘to put together’)
------------------------------------------
It is a mixture of freshly boiled milk mixed with sour milk or curds of the preceding night’s milking, offered as obla-tion to इन्द्र (or महेन्द्र) in sacrifices like the Darśa, by one who has performed सोमयाग.
Some authorities allow its offering even to those who have not performed the सोमयाग.

Saṁjñā
------------------------------------------
Saṁjñā was the daughter of Viśva-कर्म, the architect of the Gods. She was also known as Sureṇu.
Married to सूर्य (the Sun-god) she bore him two sons (Vaivasvata and यम) and a daughter (Yamunā).
Unable to bear the brilliance of सूर्य, she one day left him, after leaving her shadow-goddess called Chāyādevī in her place. Chāyādevī bore सूर्य two sons—Sāvarṇi-मनु and Śanaiścara.
When सूर्य discovered the truth he went in search of her and found her roaming about as a mare.
The two अश्विन्स् were born to them by their union.
He brought her back after pacifying her. (vide Harivaṁśa 1.9)
As a general word सṁज्ञा means a symbol as also चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.

saṁśaya
(‘that which sleeps [or remains in the मिन्द्]")
------------------------------------------
Saṁśaya or doubt is created when two kinds of knowledge, opposed to each other, arise in the मिन्द्.
In the Yogasūtras (1.30) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.), it is listed as one of the nine obstacles to योग. It has to be overcome by faith in the scripture and the teacher.
The Bhagavadgītā (4.40) declares that a doubting person loses this world and the next and ultimately destroys himself.
Some technical treatises classify सṁशय into seven categories such as śuddhasaṁśaya (doubt in general), dharmasaṁśaya (doubt regarding धर्म) and so on.

Saṁhitopaniṣad Brāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
This is one of the ब्राह्मणस् of the Sāmaveda available now.
It is said to have the characteristics of a Saṁhitā, a ब्राह्मण and an Upaniṣad. (See VEDAS.) Hence the name.
It has five khaṇḍas or sections. The following are the brief contents:
First Khaṇḍa
This contains an exposition of three kinds of sāmagāna as दैव, āsura and ārṣa.
Second Khaṇḍa
In this section a number of technical terms like karṣaṇa (prolonging a syllable in a chant by inserting more tones), स्तोभ (musical interjections like hā u, hāi, hum) as also the characteristics of a yajamāna (the sacrificer) and the उद्गातृ (main singer of the sāmans) are explained.
Third Khaṇḍa
Ūhas (See SĀMAVEDA.) to be sung in sacrifices are described here. It is also stressed that the sāmans are to be taught only to worthy candidates. Six rules concerning the teaching of the sāmans are also described.
Fourth and Fifth Khaṇḍas
The subjects discussed here include the greatness of the गुरु (preceptor) and the qualifications of a disciple, गुरु-दक्षिणा or the fees to be paid to the teacher and how a मन्त्र becomes a सामन्.
Two commentaries—one by सायण (A.
-1387) and another by Dvijarāja-bhaṭṭa—are available on this work.

Saṁnyāsopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor Upaniṣad belonging to the Atharvaveda. There are two chapters. The first chapter consists of only one prose passage. The second is a long one comprising 123 sections, mostly in anuṣṭubh verses, interspersed with passages in prose also.
First Chapter
This describes how a householder who has successfully completed all his duties should proceed to take सṁन्यास. The various steps are: taking the approval of wife and children for his सṁन्यास; performing वैश्वानर sacrifice and gifting away his possessions; withdrawing the Agnidevatā from the Vedic fires; giving up the śikhā (tuft of hair) and यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread), going away either towards the east or towards the north.
He can accept भिक्षा (alms of cooked ड़ोओद्) from all castes, using the cupped hands as the bowl. He should not hanker for tasty ड़ोओद् nor live in any place for more than one to five days. During the rainy season, however, he can stay in one place for two to four months. He should manage with minimum possessions like a bowl for alms, kaupīna (loin cloth), kanthā (wrapper), कमण्डलु (water pot), पवित्र (straining cloth), दण्ड (staff) and pādukā (sandals).
Acquiring spiritual wisdom and meditation on the आत्मन् (or God) should be his only concern.
Second Chapter
This is a very long section. The subjects dealt with may be briefly summarised as follows: persons who are fit and unfit for सṁन्यास; method of accepting सṁन्यास by giving up the śikhā and the यज्ञोपवीत and taking the accessories like the दण्ड and कमण्डलु; categories of saṁnyāsins like वैराग्य saṁnyāsins and ज्ञान saṁnyāsins as also कुटीचक and बहूदक; method of meditating on the unity of one’s आत्मन् with ब्रह्मन्; praise of citiśakti or pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्; experience of the abheda-anubhava or the non-dual state; method of taking आतुर-सṁन्यास or सṁन्यास by a dying person; meditation on one’s own true nature as the only duty of a saṁnyāsin; code of conduct including the methods of भिक्षा (begging for ड़ोओद्); prohibited things, behavior and actions; six kinds of sins like sleeping by day and acquiring disciples; expiations like prānāyāma for transgressions; continuous जप of Om (12,000 times) leading to illumination.
The only commentary available now is that by Upaniṣad-brahmendra-yogin.
There is another Saṁnyāsopaniṣad which is much smaller, comprising five sections in prose.

Saṁskṛta
(‘the refined’)
------------------------------------------
The word is generally used to indicate the सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे.
See SANSKRIT LANGUAGE for details.
